definition: A credit default swap lets a lower-credit-quality party effectively buy "credit insurance" by swapping their credit risk exposure for that of a higher-credit-quality counterparty, though the CDS itself doesn't remove credit risk entirely.
core_idea: A CDS transfers credit exposure to a third party rather than eliminating it — the buyer is still exposed if the CDS issuer itself defaults.
key_points: CDS trades exchange the credit quality associated with a risk for that of a better-rated counterparty.
CDS trades do not eliminate credit risk outright — there remains a chance the CDS issuer itself fails to pay.
relationships: Mitigation tool related to counterparty credit risk
trading_implications: Using a CDS to manage credit exposure introduces new counterparty risk on the CDS issuer, so it shifts rather than removes risk.
caveats: Buying a CDS does not fully eliminate credit risk; it substitutes the original counterparty's credit risk for the CDS issuer's.
